title: Quantum Bayes Correlated Equilibrium and the Comparison of Quantum Information Structures in Games
abstract: Bergemann and Morris (2016) show that one information structure is more informative than another exactly when it induces a smaller set of Bayes correlated equilibrium outcomes in every game. We build the quantum analogue. An information structure becomes a family of density operators indexed by the payoff state, which the mediator observes. We show that obedience is equivalent to a Loewner domination between operators on one player's subsystem. The equilibrium set is then a nonempty compact spectrahedron computable by semidefinite programming, classical structures embed exactly, and under quantum individual sufficiency more information shrinks the equilibrium set in every game.
summary: This work quantizes the comparison of information structures by defining Quantum Bayes Correlated Equilibrium (QBCE). It shows that more detailed information, modeled via a parameter $\gamma$, systematically shrinks the set of possible equilibrium outcomes and lowers the maximum achievable welfare. The methodology relies on translating complex quantum constraints into computable semidefinite programming problems.
main_problem: The paper builds a quantum analogue of comparing information structures used in games of incomplete information, aiming to quantify how much more informative one structure is compared to another.
main_result: It establishes that under quantum individual sufficiency, increasing the available information (via the mediator's observation) shrinks the set of possible Quantum Bayes Correlated Equilibrium outcomes and reduces the maximum attainable welfare in every game.
method: The authors characterize obedience using a Loewner domination condition between operators on a player's subsystem, allowing the equilibrium set to be computed as a compact spectrahedron via semidefinite programming (SDP).
model_or_system: The model is an extension of classical Bayesian games into quantum settings, where private information is encoded in subsystems and observed by a mediator. The analysis uses general quantum information structures defined by families of density operators.
key_observables: The equilibrium set (a non-empty compact spectrahedron), the maximum average welfare achievable over the QBCE set, and various comparison relations ($\preceq_{	ext{QIS}}$).
important_parameters: A depolarizing parameter $\gamma \in [0, 1]$ is used to interpolate between different information structures, controlling the amount of noise or information retained.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on defining quantum individual sufficiency and comparing structures via Loewner domination; exact equivalence with classical constraints holds only under specific conditions (e.g., simultaneous diagonalizability).
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the maximum average welfare per player as a non-increasing function of the depolarizing parameter $\gamma$, showing plateaus and subsequent drops.
paper_structure: The paper develops the QBCE concept, proves the Loewner characterization for obedience, establishes that the equilibrium set is an SDP-computable spectrahedron, and finally proves the comparison theorem by analyzing how information structure parameters ($\gamma$) affect welfare maximization.
why_interesting: While not directly about AMO systems, the mathematical tools—such as using operator inequalities (Loewner order) to constrain quantum decision processes—are highly relevant for modeling open quantum systems or measurement back-action in quantum control theory.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Maximum average welfare per player over QBCE(G, Qγ) along the de- polarizing chain of Proposition 10.1, each marker being the optimal value of a semi- definite program. Informativeness increases with γ, so the structures are ordered from least informative on the left to most informative on the right. The value is non-increasing, as Theorem 9.4 requires: more information admits fewer equilibrium outcomes and hence a lower best case. It equals 4/3, the maximum over BCE(G, S∅), for γ ≲0.33, where the obedience constraints are slack, and falls to 1 at γ = 1. The first-best value 14/9 is never attained, because joint investment in the bad state is not obedient
